text.tspan: Chapter 9: Confidence Intervals
Figure 9.4
: Large sample sizes lead to narrower intervals.
Less intuitive is the idea that lowering our confidence allows us to use a smaller margin of error. It
makes more sense when you turn it around. If you have a very small interval with a tiny margin of error,
you might feel less confident about it. Which of the following two intervals do you have more
confidence in?
1) The mean age of a college student is between 20.1 and 20.2 years of age.
2) The mean age of a college student is between 7 and 55 years of age.
Given the choice, you probably feel far more confident that the second statement is true. The first
statement might be true, but since the interval is so small, you probably feel less confident about it.
Assume you are having a party, and you want to be confident that the average attendee is happy. When
you plan the choice of drinks, you can offer a narrow choice or a wide assortment of drinks. If you have
a narrow choice of drinks, say regular and diet cola, you can’t have a high level of confidence that the
average person will like their drink. On the other hand, if you offer a wide array of choices, root-beer, 2
brands of diet and regular cola, orange drink, lemonade, iced tea, sparkling water, and juice boxes, you
can be confident that every person will have a choice they like. The analogy is that you have lower
confidence for a narrower interval, and higher confidence for a wider interval. See
